Let a dominated finite-dimensional parametric model be quadratic-mean
differentiable, with the supplied density family of [[def-qmd-path]], at an interior point $\theta_0\in\mathbb R^d$, with score
$s_{\theta_0}\in L^2(P_{\theta_0};\mathbb R^d)$. Then
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}=0$.

Fix $\tau>0$, $0\le q<1$ and $\beta>1$. Let $n\ge1$, $p\ge2$,
$p\ge n^\beta$ and $a=\log(p)/n\le1$. For iid observations from
$\mathcal P_q(\tau,c)$ of [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]], use
[[alg-entrywise-thresholded-sample-covariance]] with
$\lambda=8192\tau\sqrt a$. There is $C=C(q,\tau)<\infty$ such that
$$\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_q(\tau,c)}\mathbb E_{P^{\otimes n}}\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\le C\{c^2a^{1-q}+a\}.$$
The estimator uses sample centering and divisor $n$, including unknown means;
no independence between coordinates is assumed. This is the unmodified
threshold estimator, not a clipped version.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law
$P_{\theta_0}$ in a dominated parametric model
$\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$, where $\Theta$ is open in $\mathbb R^d$,
$d\ge1$, and $\theta_0\in\Theta$. Let $p_\theta$ be densities with respect
to one supplied sigma-finite measure. Suppose the model is QMD at $\theta_0$
with score $s_{\theta_0}$ and positive-definite information
$I=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$. Assume there are a
neighborhood $V$ of $\theta_0$ and a nonnegative measurable $L$ with
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}L^2<\infty$ such that, on one $P_{\theta_0}$-full set,
$$
|\log p_{\theta_1}(x)-\log p_{\theta_2}(x)|\le L(x)\|\theta_1-\theta_2\| \qquad(\theta_1,\theta_2\in V).
$$
Suppose a measurable exact MLE $\hat\theta_n$ exists and is consistent, in
the sense that $P_{\theta_0}(\|\hat\theta_n-\theta_0\|>\varepsilon)\to0$
for every $\varepsilon>0$. Then
$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)=I^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n s_{\theta_0}(X_i)+o_{P_{\theta_0}}(1)\ \Rightarrow\ N_d(0,I^{-1}).$$
Under the same local hypotheses, every consistent measurable exact likelihood
maximizer over a possibly $n$-dependent subset that contains $\theta_0$ is
also root-$n$ bounded in probability.
The conclusion is asymptotic; it gives no exact finite-sample normal law.

Assume AC. Fix $\beta>1$, $M,\tau>0$, and $0\le q<1$. For all integers
$n\ge1$, $p\ge2$ with $p\ge n^\beta$, and every radius
$$0\le c=c_{n,p}\le M n^{(1-q)/2}(\log p)^{-(3-q)/2},$$
put $a=\log(p)/n$ and $r_{n,p}=c^2a^{1-q}+a$. Over the law class
$\mathcal P_q(\tau,c)$ of [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]], the
minimax squared operator risk of [[def-minimax-squared-operator-risk]] satisfies
$$C_1\min\{1,r_{n,p}\}\le\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal P_q(\tau,c))\le C_2\min\{1,r_{n,p}\},$$
where $0<C_1\le C_2<\infty$ depend only on $\beta,M,\tau,q$.
For $a\le1$, the unmodified estimator of
[[alg-entrywise-thresholded-sample-covariance]], with
$\lambda=8192\tau\sqrt a$, has expected squared operator risk at most
$C(q,\tau)r_{n,p}$. A rule attaining the capped upper bound in every
dimension is explicit: use that estimator when $r_{n,p}<1$, and output
the zero matrix when $r_{n,p}\ge1$. All original dimension regimes,
including super-exponential $p$, are retained; the risk saturates instead
of diverging. The raw threshold estimator alone is not claimed to attain
the cap outside its stated regime.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid from $\mathcal P_q(\tau,c_{n,p})$ of [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]], with $n\ge1$, $p\ge2$, and $\tau>0$. Let $u>0$ and let $\widehat\Sigma^\ast$ be the sample-centered covariance. Then
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le j,k\le p}|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}| \le192\tau\left(\sqrt{\frac un}+\frac un\right)\right)\ge1-2pe^{-u}-2p^2e^{-2u}.$$
In particular $u=\log(8p^4)$ gives the original probability $1-p^{-2}$.
No independence between coordinates of a single observation is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC), as required by the library's multivariate iid central limit theorem. Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $\theta_0\in\Theta$. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid $\mathcal X$-valued observations with law $P$. Let $\psi:\Theta\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly measurable and satisfy $P\|\psi_\theta\|<\infty$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$; write $\psi_\theta(x)=\psi(\theta,x)$. Let $\hat\theta_n:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\Theta,\mathcal B(\Theta))$ be a measurable estimator sequence as in [[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]] and a Z-estimator as in [[def-z-estimator]], with the stronger root-rate condition below. Write
$$P\psi_\theta=\mathbb E[\psi_\theta(X_1)],\qquad P_n\psi_\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_\theta(X_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n\psi_\theta=\sqrt n(P_n-P)\psi_\theta.$$
Assume the displayed random vectors and suprema below are measurable, and suppose:

1. $\|\hat\theta_n-\theta_0\|=o_P(1)$ and $\sqrt n\,\|P_n\psi_{\hat\theta_n}\|=o_P(1)$.
2. $P\psi_{\theta_0}=0$, $P\|\psi_{\theta_0}\|^2<\infty$, and $\Sigma=P[\psi_{\theta_0}\psi_{\theta_0}^{T}]$.
3. The mean map $\Psi(\theta)=P\psi_\theta$ has expansion $\Psi(\theta_0+h)=Vh+\rho(h)$ with $V$ nonsingular and $\|\rho(h)\|/\|h\|\to0$ as $h\to0$, $h\ne0$.
4. The local stochastic-equicontinuity condition holds: for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\limsup_{n\to\infty}P^n\!\left(\sup_{\theta\in\Theta:\,\|\theta-\theta_0\|<\delta}\|\mathbb G_n(\psi_\theta-\psi_{\theta_0})\|>\varepsilon\right)=0.$$

Here $P^n$ denotes the product sampling law of $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$.

Then
$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)=-V^{-1}\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}+o_P(1)\Rightarrow N_d(0,V^{-1}\Sigma V^{-T}).$$
This theorem assumes consistency and the local empirical-process condition; it asserts neither. The local equicontinuity condition is the direct process hypothesis used in the proof, and consistency alone does not replace it.

At a fixed one-dimensional interior point, suppose the design density is
positive and $C^2$ locally, the chosen regression function is $C^2$ locally,
and the conditional response variance is finite and continuous. Suppose
$K$ is nonnegative, symmetric, positive near zero, normalized, with finite
positive second moment and finite squared integral. If $h_n\to0$,
$nh_n\to\infty$ and $nh_n^3\to\infty$, then the empirical local-linear fit
with a fixed fallback only on singular designs has a Lebesgue expectation
(and hence an unconditional second-order mean-bias expansion).

Symmetry of the kernel alone makes the population Nadaraya–Watson smoother
reproduce every affine regression function exactly in the interior and keeps
its bias of order $h^2$ at a support boundary.

Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix $n\ge1$, a point
$x\in\mathbb R$, bandwidth $h>0$, degree $p\in\mathbb N_0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K$, and fallback $a_0\in\mathbb R$. Set
$u_i=(x-X_i)/h$, $r_p(u)=(1,u,\ldots,u^p)^\mathsf T$, let $Z$ be the matrix
whose $i$th row is $r_p(u_i)^\mathsf T$, let
$W=\operatorname{diag}(K(u_1),\ldots,K(u_n))$, and put
$M=Z^\mathsf TWZ$. If $M$ is nonsingular, define
$$\widehat\beta=M^{-1}Z^\mathsf TW(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^\mathsf T,\qquad \widehat m_{p,h}(x)=\widehat\beta_0.$$
If $M$ is singular, define $\widehat m_{p,h}(x)=a_0$. For fixed $x,h,n,p$
and Borel $K$, this is a real statistic estimating the pointwise target
$m(x)$ as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The case $p=1$ is the
**local-linear estimator**. No claim that $M$ is nonsingular for a given
sample is implicit in this definition.

Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix a sample size $n\ge1$,
a prediction point $x\in\mathbb R$, a bandwidth $h>0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$, and a fixed fallback
$a_0\in\mathbb R$. For data $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$, put
$$D_{n,h}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h).$$
The **Nadaraya–Watson estimator** of the pointwise target $m(x)$ is
$$\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h}(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h)Y_i}{D_{n,h}(x)},&D_{n,h}(x)>0,\\[6pt] a_0,&D_{n,h}(x)=0. \end{cases}$$
For fixed $x,h,n$, this is a statistic of the observed sample with real target
$m(x)$, in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The fallback is part
of the definition. Kernel regularity and bandwidth assumptions used for bias
or variance results are stated in those results.

Assume AC as used to select the regression version. Fix a statistical experiment indexed by $\theta$, a point $x$, a real
regression target $m_\theta(x)$, and a real-valued estimator
$T_x$ of that target, meaning a measurable statistic with target space
$\mathbb R$ as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. At this point, use the
squared-error loss
$$L_x(\theta,a)=(a-m_\theta(x))^2,\qquad a\in\mathbb R.$$
Its **pointwise squared-error risk** is the possibly infinite quantity
$$R_x(\theta,T_x)=\int (T_x(z)-m_\theta(x))^2\,P_\theta(dz)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is the deterministic-rule specialization of the risk in
[[def-loss-function-and-risk]]: the action space is $\mathbb R$ with its
Borel sigma-algebra, the action is $T_x(z)$, and the loss section is
measurable because it is continuous in $a$. The integral is nonnegative, so
it is defined without a finite-moment assumption.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real random variables on a probability
space, with $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$, and choose a regular conditional law
$Q(x,dy)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$. On
$D=\{x:\int |y|\,Q(x,dy)<\infty\}$ define
$m(x)=\int y\,Q(x,dy)$, and put $m(x)=0$ off $D$. By
[[cor-conditional-expectation-as-a-measurable-function-of-the-conditioning-variable]],
$m$ is Borel measurable and $m(X)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E[Y\mid\sigma(X)]$. A **regression target** is the resulting
$P_X$-almost-sure equivalence class; a **chosen regression-function version**
is the particular Borel function selected by the specified conditional law.

Pointwise smoothness is an additional hypothesis on the chosen version. It is
not implied by existence of conditional expectation, and statements about
$m(x)$ at a specified point use that selected version.

Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Let $X,Y$ be real random
variables with $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$ and $Y=a+bX$ almost surely. Choose the
regular conditional law $Q(t,dy)=\delta_{a+bt}(dy)$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$;
then the chosen regression-function version is $m(t)=a+bt$ at every point.
For any observed sample and any $x,h$ whose degree-one local moment matrix is
nonsingular, the local-linear estimate equals $a+bx$, even when the design
points are asymmetric around $x$.

Let $X_i$ be iid real random variables with density $f$ continuous and
positive at a fixed point $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative,
symmetric, with $\int K=1$ and $0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$.
Assume compact kernel support, a globally bounded density $f$, or a bounded
rapid-tail kernel satisfying $\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)\to0$.
For $h=h_n\to0$ with $nh_n\to\infty$, set $U_i=(x-X_i)/h_n$ and
$$M_n=\frac1{nh_n}\sum_{i=1}^nK(U_i)\begin{pmatrix}1\\U_i\end{pmatrix}(1,U_i).$$
Then
$$M_n\longrightarrow f(x)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\mu_2\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{in probability},$$
and $\mathbb P(M_n\text{ is nonsingular})\to1$.
More generally, the proof establishes $(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_i L(U_i)\to f(x)\int L$
for any integrable Borel function $L$, if $f$ is bounded globally or $L$
has compact support. Boundedness or square integrability of $L$ is unnecessary.

Assume AC for the chosen regression version. Let $X_i$ be independent and
identically distributed with density $f$ continuous and positive at an
interior point $x$. For the chosen conditional law $Q(t,dy)$ in
[[def-regression-target-version]], set
$\sigma^2(t)=\int (y-m(t))^2Q(t,dy)$ where finite. Conditional on the
predictor vector, assume the responses are independent, have means $m(X_i)$,
and have variances $\sigma^2(X_i)$, where $\sigma^2$ is finite and continuous
at $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative, symmetric, with $\int K=1$,
$0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$ and $R(K)=\int K^2<\infty$.
Assume compact kernel support, globally bounded $f,\sigma^2$, or the
rapid-tail alternative: $\mathbb E Y^2<\infty$, bounded $K$, and
$\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)\to0$. In this last alternative the stated
local continuity is sufficient.
For the local-linear conclusion also assume $\int u^2K(u)^2\,du<\infty$;
this extra squared moment is automatic for compactly supported kernels.
The Nadaraya–Watson conclusion requires only $R(K)<\infty$. For $h_n\to0$ with $nh_n\to\infty$, use the fixed
fallbacks in [[def-nadaraya-watson-estimator]] and
[[def-local-polynomial-estimator]]. Then, with variance taken conditionally
on $X_1,\ldots,X_n$,
$$nh_n\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h_n}(x)\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n) \longrightarrow \frac{R(K)\sigma^2(x)}{f(x)} \quad\text{in probability},$$
and the same limit holds with $\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h_n}(x)$ replaced by
the degree-one local-linear estimator. This is a conditional-variance
statement for both estimators. If additionally $m$ is continuous at $x$
and bounded globally (only bounded near $x$ is required for compact $K$),
or if the rapid-tail alternative holds and $m$ is continuous at $x$,
with $nh_n^3\to\infty$ additionally in this rapid-tail unconditional clause,
then the Nadaraya–Watson estimator is square-integrable for large $n$ and
$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h_n}(x))=\frac{R(K)\sigma^2(x)}{nh_nf(x)}+o((nh_n)^{-1}).$$
No unconditional local-linear variance is asserted: near-singular designs
can make even its finite-sample expectation undefined.

Assume AC for the chosen regression version. Let $X_i$ be iid with density
$f$, with $f(x)>0$ at a fixed interior point $x$, and let $f,m$ be $C^2$
near $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative and symmetric, with
$\int K=1$, $0<\mu_2=\int u^2K<\infty$ and
$\int(1+u^2)K(u)^2\,du<\infty$. Assume either compact kernel support, or
that $f,m$ and their first two derivatives are bounded and continuous
globally. A further localization alternative, including the Gaussian kernel, is that
$\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty$, $K$ is bounded, and
$$\lim_{A\to\infty}\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)=0.$$
Under this rapid-tail alternative only the stated local smoothness of
$f,m$ is needed; no global boundedness of $m$ or of its derivatives is assumed.
Let $h_n\to0$ with $nh_n^3\to\infty$. For almost every realized design,
integrate the degree-one fit of [[def-local-polynomial-estimator]] against
the independent response laws $\prod_iQ(X_i,dy_i)$; call the resulting
finite response-law mean $b_n(x)$, with the same fixed fallback on singular
designs. Then
$$b_n(x)-m(x)=\frac{h_n^2\mu_2}{2}m''(x)+o_P(h_n^2).$$
Here $Z_n=o_P(h_n^2)$ means $Z_n/h_n^2\to0$ in probability. This is a
conditional response-law mean statement; it neither assumes nor asserts
that the estimator has an unconditional Lebesgue expectation.

Assume AC for the chosen regression version [[def-regression-target-version]].
Let $X$ have density $f$, with $f(x)>0$ at a fixed interior point $x$,
and let $f,m$ be $C^2$ near $x$. Let $K$ be a finite-valued Borel,
nonnegative symmetric kernel with $\int K=1$,
$0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$ and $\int K^2<\infty$.
Assume either compact kernel support, or that $f,m$ and their first two
derivatives are bounded and continuous on $\mathbb R$.
A further localization alternative, including the Gaussian kernel, is that
$\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty$, $K$ is bounded, and
$$\lim_{A\to\infty}\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)=0.$$
Under this rapid-tail alternative only the stated local smoothness of
$f,m$ is needed; no global boundedness of $m$ or of its derivatives is assumed.
Set
$$S_j(h)=\int K(u)u^j f(x-hu)\,du,\qquad T_j(h)=\int K(u)u^j f(x-hu)m(x-hu)\,du.$$
For sufficiently small $h$, $D_h=S_0S_2-S_1^2>0$ and the population
local-linear intercept, in the coordinates of [[def-local-polynomial-estimator]], is
$$m_{\mathrm{LL},h}(x)=\frac{S_2T_0-S_1T_1}{D_h}.$$
Then
$$m_{\mathrm{LL},h}(x)-m(x)=\frac{h^2\mu_2}{2}m''(x)+o(h^2).$$
This requires no fourth kernel moment.

Assume AC for the chosen regression version. Let $X_i$ be iid with density
$f$, and, conditional on the predictors, let the responses be independent
with the selected conditional laws $Q(X_i,dy)$, means $m(X_i)$ and variances
$\sigma^2(X_i)$. At a fixed interior point $x$, suppose $f(x)>0$, $f,m$ are
$C^2$ near $x$, and $\sigma^2$ is finite and continuous at $x$.
Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative, symmetric, positive on some
neighborhood of zero, with $\int K=1$, $0<\mu_2=\int u^2K<\infty$ and
$R(K)=\int K^2<\infty$. Assume either compact kernel support, or that
$f,m$ and their first two derivatives are bounded and continuous globally
and $\sigma^2$ is finite and bounded globally. A further localization alternative, including the Gaussian kernel, is that
$\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty$, $K$ is bounded, and
$$\lim_{A\to\infty}\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)=0.$$
Under this rapid-tail alternative only the stated local smoothness of
$f,m$ is needed; no global boundedness of $m$ or of its derivatives is assumed.
For $h_n\to0$ with
$nh_n^3\to\infty$, and any fixed finite fallback, the estimator in
[[def-nadaraya-watson-estimator]] is integrable for all sufficiently large
$n$ and
$$\mathbb E[\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h_n}(x)]-m(x)=\frac{h_n^2\mu_2}{2}\left(m''(x)+2m'(x)\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\right)+o(h_n^2).$$
The compact/global alternatives require no boundedness or continuity of $K$.

Assume AC for the chosen regression version [[def-regression-target-version]].
Let $X$ have Lebesgue density $f$, with $f(x)>0$ at a fixed interior point
$x$, and let $f,m$ be $C^2$ near $x$. Let $K$ be a finite-valued Borel,
nonnegative, symmetric kernel with $\int K=1$,
$0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$ and $\int K^2<\infty$.
Assume either that $K$ has compact support, or that $f,m$ and their first
two derivatives are bounded and continuous on $\mathbb R$. In these first two alternatives, no continuity
or boundedness of $K$ is required. The global alternative supplies tail
control for noncompact kernels; local smoothness alone does not supply it.
A further localization alternative, including the Gaussian kernel, is that
$\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty$, $K$ is bounded, and
$$\lim_{A\to\infty}\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)=0.$$
Under this rapid-tail alternative only the stated local smoothness of
$f,m$ is needed; no global boundedness of $m$ or of its derivatives is assumed.
For sufficiently small $h>0$, the population smoother corresponding to
[[def-nadaraya-watson-estimator]] is well defined by
$$m_h(x)=\frac{\int K(u)m(x-hu)f(x-hu)\,du}{\int K(u)f(x-hu)\,du},$$
and
$$m_h(x)-m(x)=\frac{h^2\mu_2}{2}\left(m''(x)+2m'(x)\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\right)+o(h^2).$$

Assume AC as used to select the regression target version. Fix a model
parameter $\theta$ and point $x$. Let $T_x$ be a real estimator of the finite
target $\psi=m_\theta(x)$ with $\mathbb E_\theta[T_x^2]<\infty$. Define its
bias by $b_\theta(x)=\mathbb E_\theta[T_x]-m_\theta(x)$. Its pointwise
squared-error risk from [[def-pointwise-regression-risk]] satisfies
$$R_x(\theta,T_x)=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T_x)+b_\theta(x)^2.$$

Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval and let $a\le t_1<\cdots<t_r\le b$ with $r\ge2$. A natural cubic spline with knots $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ is a $C^2$ function on $[a,b]$ that is a polynomial of degree at most three on every $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, has second derivative zero at $t_1$ and $t_r$, and is extended linearly on $[a,t_1]$ and $[t_r,b]$ when those intervals are nonempty. The knots $t_j$ are the distinct breakpoints; repeated observations at the same input do not create additional knots.

Fix a degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$, an exponent $1\le q\le\infty$, and an integer $0\le l\le p$. A **local quasi-interpolant** is a linear map $Q$ from continuous $L^q$ functions on $[a,b]$ into $S_{p,\xi}$ with the following properties. For every nonempty knot interval $I_m$, there is a neighborhood $J_m\subseteq[a,b]$ that is a union of at most $M$ adjacent knot intervals such that (i) if $f=g$ almost everywhere on $J_m$, then $Qf=Qg$ almost everywhere on $I_m$; (ii) $Qv=v$ for every $v\in\mathcal P_l$; and (iii) for a constant $C_Q$ independent of the mesh, $\|Qf\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le C_Q\|f\|_{L^q(J_m)}$. Here $M$ bounds both the number of intervals in each $J_m$ and the number of neighborhoods $J_m$ containing any one point. The derivative and continuous-representative conventions for Sobolev inputs are those of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]].

The coefficient-functional formulation in Lyche–Manni–Speleers is one sufficient way to obtain these local stability and reproduction properties. The definition here records the operator hypotheses used in the approximation proof.

Let $r\ge2$, $a\le x_1<\cdots<x_r\le b$, and $y_1,\ldots,y_r\in\mathbb R$. There is exactly one natural cubic spline $s$ on $[a,b]$ with $s(x_i)=y_i$ for each $i$. On each interval $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ it is the cubic with endpoint values $y_i,y_{i+1}$ and endpoint second derivatives $M_i,M_{i+1}$, where $M_1=M_r=0$ and the interior values solve the positive-definite tridiagonal system
$$h_{i-1}M_{i-1}+2(h_{i-1}+h_i)M_i+h_iM_{i+1}=6\left(\frac{y_{i+1}-y_i}{h_i}-\frac{y_i-y_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}\right),\quad 2\le i\le r-1,$$
with $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$. The interpolant is linear outside $[x_1,x_r]$.

Let $p_K(x)=(B_{1,p,\xi}(x),\ldots,B_{K,p,\xi}(x))^T$ be a specified degree-$p$ B-spline basis on the data domain, and let $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be observed real-valued data. Form the design matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times K}$ with row $p_K(X_i)^T$. The **series least-squares fitted training vector** is
$$\widehat{\mathbf g}_K=\Pi_{\operatorname{col}(P)}\mathbf Y,$$
the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^T$ onto the column space of $P$. Conditional on the realized design, this is the fixed-design least-squares fitted vector of [[def-fixed-design-projection-estimator]]. Equivalently, it is $P\widehat\beta$ for any minimizer $\widehat\beta$ of $\|\mathbf Y-P\beta\|_2^2$; all such minimizers have the same fitted training vector. The training prediction loss relative to a specified target vector $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$ is $n^{-1}\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2$. This definition specifies training fitted values and makes no test-risk assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $[a,b]$, $\lambda>0$, and data $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ satisfy the hypotheses of [[def-natural-cubic-smoothing-spline]], with $r\ge2$ distinct inputs $t_1<\cdots<t_r$. Then $J$ has a unique minimizer over $W^{2,2}(a,b)$. It is the natural cubic spline with knots at $t_1,\ldots,t_r$, extended linearly to $a$ and $b$ where needed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $p\ge0$, $0\le l\le p$, $1\le q\le\infty$, and let $Q$ be a bounded local quasi-interpolant as in [[def-local-spline-quasi-interpolant]] on a knot mesh in $[a,b]$. Let $f\in W^{l+1,q}(a,b)$ and use its continuous Sobolev representative. For each nonempty mesh cell $I_m$, let $J_m$ be the corresponding neighborhood, let $h_m$ be the largest cell length in $J_m$, and suppose $|J_m|\le M h_m$ with overlap multiplicity at most $M$. Then
$$\|f-Qf\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le (1+C_Q)\frac{M^{l+1}}{l!}h_m^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q(J_m)}.$$
Writing $h=\max_m h_m$, the global bound is
$$\|f-Qf\|_{L^q([a,b])}\le (1+C_Q)\frac{M^{l+1+1/q}}{l!}h^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q([a,b])},$$
where $1/q=0$ for $q=\infty$. In particular, on a uniform mesh with interior knots of multiplicity $p+1$, the cellwise $L^2$ projector onto $\mathcal P_p$ is a local quasi-interpolant and gives the order-$h^s$ approximation bound for every integer $1\le s\le p+1$.

Let $n,K\ge1$, let $X_i\in[a,b]$ and $Y_i\in\mathbb R$ be iid pairs, and suppose the one-observation law is $P_X(dx)\kappa(x,dy)$ for a supplied Borel probability kernel $\kappa$ from $([a,b],\mathcal B([a,b]))$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Assume a Borel function $g_0:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is supplied such that, for $P_X$-almost every $x$, $\int |y|\,\kappa(x,dy)<\infty$, $g_0(x)=\int y\,\kappa(x,dy)$, and $\int (y-g_0(x))^2\,\kappa(x,dy)\le\Delta$ for a finite $\Delta\ge0$. Let $p_K:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^K$ be a fixed Borel $K$-dimensional spline basis and assume a deterministic $\bar\beta_K\in\mathbb R^K$ and constants $C,\gamma>0$ satisfy
$$E\{g_0(X)-p_K(X)^T\bar\beta_K\}^2\le C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
Then, with the fitted training vector $\widehat{\mathbf g}_K$ from [[def-series-spline-least-squares]] and $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$,
$$E\left[\frac1n\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2\right]\le\frac{\Delta K}{n}+C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
This is expected empirical training-design loss.

Assume AC. Let $X,Y$ be real random variables with $E|Y|<\infty$, choose a regular conditional law $Q(x,dy)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$, and let $g_0$ be the selected Borel regression-function version from [[def-regression-target-version]]. Suppose $P_X$ is supported on $[a,b]$ with density bounded by $M_X$, $g_0\in W^{s,2}(a,b)$ for an integer $s\ge1$, and $\int (y-g_0(x))^2Q(x,dy)\le\Delta$ for $P_X$-almost every $x$. For degree $p\ge s-1$, use a uniform partition into $J$ cells and the B-spline space with each interior knot repeated $p+1$ times, so its dimension is $K=(p+1)J$. For iid observations from this joint law, let $\widehat{\mathbf g}_K$ be the fitted training vector and $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$. Then
$$E\left[\frac1n\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2\right]\le\frac{\Delta K}{n}+C_{s,p,M_X,a,b}\,K^{-2s}\|D^sg_0\|_{L^2(a,b)}^2.$$
Choosing $J\asymp n^{1/(2s+1)}$ (equivalently $K\asymp n^{1/(2s+1)}$ for fixed $p$) gives expected empirical training risk $O(n^{-2s/(2s+1)})$. This is not an independent-test-risk bound.
The formula $\sum_i(y_i-g(x_i))^2+\lambda\int_a^b|D^2g|^2$ has a unique minimizing function for every nonempty data set whenever $\lambda>0$, including data with only one distinct input.

Take degree $p=2$ and clamped knot vector $(0,0,0,1,1,1)$. On $[0,1]$ its three B-splines are $(1-x)^2$, $2x(1-x)$, and $x^2$. They form a nonnegative partition of unity and hence a basis of $\mathcal P_2$.

With two knots, the natural cubic interpolant is the line joining the two values. With knots $0,1,2$ and values $0,1,0$, the middle second derivative is $-3$, and the interpolant is
$$s(x)=\begin{cases}\frac32x-\frac12x^3,&0\le x\le1,\\[2pt]\frac32(2-x)-\frac12(2-x)^3,&1\le x\le2.\end{cases}$$

Let $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_J=1$ be a uniform partition with mesh $h=1/J$. For $f\in W^{2,\infty}(0,1)$, its continuous representative has a piecewise-linear interpolant $I_hf$ in the degree-one spline space with simple interior knots.

Use the degree-one clamped B-spline basis $p(x)=(1-x,x)$ on $[0,1]$, with a single fixed training input $x_1=1/2$ and response $y_1=1$. The coefficient vector $\widehat\beta=(0,2)^T$ is a least-squares minimizer and gives the fitted function $\widehat g(x)=2x$. Let the target be $g_0(x)=1$ and the independent test input be uniform on $[0,1]$.

Assume AC. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable, symmetric and quasi-convex, with $M>0$. For integers $N\ge2$ and $m\ge1$, put $\delta=M/N$, $C_k=\overline{\{x:L(x)\le k\delta\}}$ and
$$g_{N,m}(x)=\delta\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\min(1,m\,d(x,C_k)).$$
For $C_k=\varnothing$ the corresponding summand is defined to be one, and for $C_k=\mathbb R^d$ it is zero. Then $0\le g_{N,m}\le L$, and $g_{N,m}$ is bounded and Lipschitz. For every nondegenerate Gaussian $H\sim N_d(b,S)$,
$$\inf_a E g_{N,m}(a-H)=E g_{N,m}(H-b),\qquad \lim_{N\to\infty}\lim_{m\to\infty}E g_{N,m}(H-b)=E L(H-b).$$
Each summand is symmetric and quasi-convex; no quasi-convexity of their sum is asserted.

Assume AC and [[def-qmd-path]] at $\theta_0$ with score $s$ and information $I$.
Let $h_n\to h$ in $\mathbb R^d$, put $u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$, and write
$P_0=P_{\theta_0}$ and $P_{u_n}=P_{\theta_0+u_n}$. On
$S=\{p_{\theta_0}>0\}$ define, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$q_n(x)=\frac{\mathbf1_S(x)p_{\theta_0+u_n}(x)} {(1-\alpha_n)p_{\theta_0}(x)},\qquad \alpha_n=P_{u_n}(S^c).$$
Then $q_n$ is a probability density relative to $P_0$. For IID
$X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, let $L_n=\prod_{i=1}^nq_n(X_i)$ and
$\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)$. Under $P_0^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad P_0^{\otimes n}(L_n=0)\to0.$$
Moreover, if $\bar P_n=q_nP_0$ is the normalized absolutely continuous
component of $P_{u_n}$ relative to $P_0$, then
$$\|P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}-\bar P_n^{\otimes n}\|_{\rm TV}\to0.$$
No full likelihood ratio for $P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}$ is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subseteq
\mathbb R^d\}$ be dominated by a common sigma-finite measure, with $\Theta$
open, and suppose the model is QMD at an interior $\theta_0$ with score $s$
and information $I=E_{\theta_0}[ss^T]$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID
$P_{\theta_0}$, and for each fixed local sequence $h_n\to h$ set
$u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$. Then the local product laws
$P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}$ admit mean-one likelihood-ratio proxies
$L_n$ relative to $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$ such that
$$\left\|P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}-L_nP_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}\right\|_{\rm TV} \to0,$$
and under $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad \Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)\Rightarrow N_d(0,I).$$
Thus the IID QMD experiment is LAN in the proxy sense of
[[def-lan-experiment]]. This assertion does not claim that the full local
product law has a Radon–Nikodym derivative relative to the base law.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID $N(\theta,1)$ and take $\theta_0=0$. This
one-dimensional model is QMD at zero with score $s(x)=x$ and information
$I=1$. For every fixed $h$, the local laws $P_{n,h}=N(h/\sqrt n,1)^{\otimes n}$
are exactly dominated by $P_{n,0}$ and
$$\log\frac{dP_{n,h}}{dP_{n,0}}(X_1,\ldots,X_n) =h\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^2,\qquad \Delta_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
The sample mean estimator is regular, with
$$\sqrt n\left(\bar X_n-\frac h{\sqrt n}\right)\Rightarrow N(0,1)$$
under $P_{n,h}$ for each fixed $h$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID from a probability law $P$ that is misspecified relative to the density family $p_\theta$, and let $\ell_\theta=\log p_\theta$ be as in [[def-pseudo-true-parameter-under-misspecification]]. Write $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nf(X_i)$ and $M(\theta)=\mathbb E_P\ell_\theta(X)$. Assume that $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, and that $\theta^*$ is the unique separated interior maximizer of $M$, where interior means that some Euclidean open ball about $\theta^*$ lies in $\Theta$: for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\eta_\varepsilon>0$ such that $M(\theta^*)-M(\theta)\ge\eta_\varepsilon$ whenever $\theta\in\Theta$ and $\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2\ge\varepsilon$. Assume the uniform law $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|P_n\ell_\theta-M(\theta)|\to_P0$, and let $\hat\theta_n\in\Theta$ be a measurable approximate maximizer with $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_n\ell_\theta-P_n\ell_{\hat\theta_n}\to_P0$.

Let $S_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta(x)$ be continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $\theta^*$. Assume $\mathbb E_PS_{\theta^*}=0$, $\mathbb E_P\|S_{\theta^*}\|_2^2<\infty$, and set $J=\mathbb E_P[S_{\theta^*}S_{\theta^*}^{T}]$. Suppose $H=\mathbb E_P[\nabla_\theta S_{\theta^*}]$ is nonsingular, $D(\theta):=\mathbb E_P[\nabla_\theta S_\theta]$ exists and is continuous at $\theta^*$, and for every sufficiently small fixed $\delta>0$,

$$\sup_{\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2\le\delta}\|P_n\nabla_\theta S_\theta-D(\theta)\|_{op}\to_P0,$$

where $\|A\|_{op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2\le1}\|Av\|_2$. Finally assume the approximate score equation $\sqrt n\,P_nS_{\hat\theta_n}=o_P(1)$. Then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta^*)\Rightarrow N_d\!\left(0,H^{-1}JH^{-T}\right).$$

The covariance is the sandwich matrix formed from the Hessian $H$ under $P$ and the score second moment $J$ under $P$. The theorem does not assert that it equals the inverse Fisher information of the fitted model.

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be one measurable space and let $P_n,Q_n$ be
probability measures on it ([[def-probability-measure]]). The sequence
$(Q_n)$ is **contiguous with respect to** $(P_n)$, written $Q_n\triangleleft
P_n$, if for every sequence $A_n\in\mathcal A$,
$$P_n(A_n)\longrightarrow0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q_n(A_n)\longrightarrow0.$$
The sequences are **mutually contiguous**, written $Q_n\triangleleft\triangleright
P_n$, if both $Q_n\triangleleft P_n$ and $P_n\triangleleft Q_n$.

Contiguity is a relation between sequences of laws, not absolute continuity at
each finite $n$. It says that events negligible under one sequence remain
negligible under the other in the indicated direction.

Assume countable choice. For every convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, its
topological boundary $\partial C=\overline C\setminus C^\circ$ has
$d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. If $C$ has empty interior, then $C$
itself is contained in a proper affine subspace and is Lebesgue null.

Let $P_{n,h}$ be probability laws on a common measurable space for each
integer $n\ge1$ and local parameter $h\in\mathbb R^d$, where $d<\infty$ and
$P_{n,0}$ is the base law. Suppose that for every fixed $h$ we are supplied a
nonnegative measurable function $L_{n,h}$ with
$$\int L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}=1.$$
It defines an absolutely continuous proxy
$$\bar P_{n,h}(A):=\int_A L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}.$$
The actual local law is allowed to have a singular part; the approximation
condition below is what connects it to this proxy.

The experiments are **locally asymptotically normal (LAN)** at $h=0$ with
information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$ if $K$ is a symmetric
positive semidefinite $d\times d$ matrix, $\Delta_n$ is an $\mathbb R^d$-valued
statistic,
$$\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)\quad\text{under }P_{n,0},$$
and for every fixed $h\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\|P_{n,h}-\bar P_{n,h}\|_{\rm TV}\to0,\qquad \log L_{n,h}=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TKh+o_{P_{n,0}}(1),$$
where $\|\cdot\|_{\rm TV}$ is the event-supremum total variation distance
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]) and
$o_{P_{n,0}}(1)$ means convergence to zero in $P_{n,0}$-probability. We set
$\log0=-\infty$; the finite-valued expansion entails
$P_{n,0}(L_{n,h}=0)\to0$. Convergence in distribution is as in
[[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]], and $N_d(0,K)$ allows
singular $K$ ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]]).

If $P_{n,h}=\bar P_{n,h}$, this is the usual dominated LAN comparison. The
proxy formulation also covers QMD paths whose local alternatives are not
absolutely continuous with respect to the base law, provided the singular
product mass tends to zero in total variation. This definition is pointwise
in each fixed $h$; it does not assert uniformity over bounded sets of $h$.

Assume countable choice. Let $d\ge1$ and let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be
nonempty compact convex sets. With $A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B\}$ and
$\lambda_d$ denoting Lebesgue measure,
$$\lambda_d(A+B)^{1/d}\ge \lambda_d(A)^{1/d}+\lambda_d(B)^{1/d}.$$
Zero-volume and lower-dimensional sets are included.

For each $n$, let $P_n,Q_n$ be probability measures on one measurable space,
and let $L_n\ge0$ satisfy $Q_n(A)=\int_A L_n\,dP_n$ for every measurable
$A$. Suppose $E_{P_n}L_n=1$, $L_n\Rightarrow L$ under $P_n$, $L\ge0$, and
$E L=1$. Then $(Q_n)$ is contiguous with respect to $(P_n)$.

In a local experiment $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ at $h=0$
([[def-lan-experiment]]), let $T_n$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued statistic.
It is **regular at zero with limit law $W$** if, for every fixed
$h\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$T_n-h\Rightarrow W\quad\text{under }P_{n,h},$$
where the same probability law $W$ works for all $h$. In a parametric model
with true parameter $\theta_0$, this is the definition for
$T_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ and local laws at
$\theta_0+h/\sqrt n$; equivalently the centered error
$\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0-h/\sqrt n)$ has a limit independent of
the fixed local displacement $h$.

Assume AC.

Let $H\subset\mathbb R^d$ be compact, let $\pi$ be a probability measure on
$H$, and let $P_{n,0}$ be base laws. Suppose $L_n(h,x)$ is jointly measurable
in $(h,x)$, nonnegative, and satisfies
$\int L_n(h,x)P_{n,0}(dx)=1$ for every $h\in H$. Let
$\Delta_n\Rightarrow Z\sim N_d(0,K)$ under $P_{n,0}$, where $K$ is positive
semidefinite, and put
$$g_h(z)=\exp(h^Tz-\tfrac12h^TKh).$$
Assume the random variable
$$a_n(x):=\sup_{h\in H}|L_n(h,x)-g_h(\Delta_n(x))|$$
is measurable and $E_{P_{n,0}}a_n\to0$. Let the prior-predictive law be
$M_n(dx)=m_n(x)P_{n,0}(dx)$ with
$m_n(x)=\int_HL_n(h,x)\pi(dh)$, and define posteriors
$$\Pi_n(dh\mid x)=\frac{L_n(h,x)\pi(dh)}{m_n(x)},\qquad \Pi^G(dh\mid z)=\frac{g_h(z)\pi(dh)}{m(z)},\quad m(z)=\int_Hg_h(z)\pi(dh),$$
where an arbitrary probability measure is assigned if a denominator is zero.
Then
$$E_{M_n}\int_H\left| \frac{L_n(h,X)}{m_n(X)}- \frac{g_h(\Delta_n(X))}{m(\Delta_n(X))} \right|\pi(dh)\longrightarrow0.$$
In particular the posterior laws converge in expected total variation,
because their event-probability differences are bounded by this $L^1(\pi)$
distance. The convention for total variation is
[[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]].

This lemma assumes an $L^1$ uniform likelihood-field approximation. Pointwise
LAN alone does not supply that hypothesis.

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$ with positive-definite covariance
$\Sigma$. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable and symmetric,
$L(-x)=L(x)$, and quasi-convex, meaning each sublevel set
$\{x:L(x)\le t\}$ is convex. Then for every $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$E L(X-a)\ge E L(X-m).$$
Thus the Gaussian center $m$ minimizes expected loss. The result includes
quasi-convex losses whose sublevel sets are not closed.

Assume AC.

Let $P_n$ be probability measures and let $Q_n=L_nP_n$, where $L_n\ge0$ and
$E_{P_n}L_n=1$. Let $T_n$ take values in $\mathbb R^k$. Suppose under $P_n$
that $(T_n,L_n)\Rightarrow(T,e^Z)$, where $Z$ is normal with mean
$-\sigma^2/2$ and variance $\sigma^2$; the joint law of $(T,Z)$ need not be
Gaussian. Then under $Q_n$, $T_n$ converges in distribution to the probability
law determined by
$$E[f(T^{(Q)})]=E[e^Zf(T)]$$
for every bounded continuous $f$. In particular, $Q_n$ is contiguous with
respect to $P_n$. If $(T,Z)$ is jointly Gaussian with
$T\sim N_k(\mu,\Sigma)$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(T,Z)=\tau$, this tilted
law is $N_k(\mu+\tau,\Sigma)$, including singular $\Sigma$.

Assume AC and a parametric model QMD at $\theta_0$ with score $s_{\theta_0}$.
Then
$$E_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}=0,$$
and the information matrix
$I_{\theta_0}=E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$ has finite entries
and is positive semidefinite. The QMD convention and square-integrability of
the score are those of [[def-qmd-path]].

Assume AC. Let $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ be LAN at $h=0$ with
positive-definite information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$.
Let $T_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ be regular under every fixed
local alternative, with common limit law $W$ as in
[[def-regular-estimator-under-local-alternatives]]. Then there is a
probability law $\nu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ such that
$$\mathcal L(W)=N_d(0,K^{-1})*\nu.$$
Here $*$ is convolution, the law of the sum of independent random vectors
with the two indicated laws. In particular, the efficient Gaussian component
with covariance $K^{-1}$ is a convolution factor of every regular limit.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[def-qmd-path]]. Write $p_0=p_{\theta_0}$,
$p_u=p_{\theta_0+u}$, and $P_0=P_{\theta_0}$. Let
$$\alpha(u):=P_{\theta_0+u}(p_0=0),\qquad \beta(u):=P_0(p_u=0).$$
Then $\alpha(u)=o(\|u\|_2^2)$ and $\beta(u)=o(\|u\|_2^2)$ as $u\to0$.

Assume AC. In a pointwise LAN experiment [[def-lan-experiment]] with $K\succ0$, fix $h_1,\ldots,h_s\in\mathbb R^d$ and weights $w_i>0$ summing to one. Let $g:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Lipschitz. The Bayes values for estimating $h$ with loss $g(a-h)$ and this finite prior, allowing all measurable randomized rules, converge to the corresponding Bayes value in the Gaussian shift $Y\mid h\sim N_d(h,K^{-1})$. No likelihood-field uniformity or measurable-selection hypothesis is required.

Assume AC. Let $Q_h=N_d(h,S)$ with $S\succ0$ and let $g:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ have Lipschitz constant $B<\infty$. For every Borel probability prior $\pi$ on $\mathbb R^d$ and $\epsilon>0$, there is a finite-support prior $\pi_f$ whose Bayes value for loss $g(a-h)$ differs from that of $\pi$ by less than $\epsilon$. The comparison is uniform over all measurable randomized rules. In particular this applies to every diffuse Gaussian prior; no posterior selector assumption is needed.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. Let $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ be a finite-dimensional
experiment that is LAN at $h=0$ with positive-definite information $K$ and
central sequence $\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)$ as in
[[def-lan-experiment]]. Let $M\ge0$ be finite and
$L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable,
symmetric ($L(-x)=L(x)$), and quasi-convex (each sublevel set is convex).
Then
$$ \liminf_{c\to\infty}\liminf_{n\to\infty} \inf_{\widehat h_n}\sup_{\|h\|_2\le c} E_{P_{n,h}}L(\widehat h_n-h) \ge E L(Z),\qquad Z\sim N_d(0,K^{-1}). $$
The infimum ranges over measurable, possibly randomized estimators. The
experiment is pointwise LAN in each fixed $h$; no uniform likelihood-field
assumption is added.

For $n\ge2$, define probability laws on $\{0,1\}$ by
$$P_n\{1\}=1/n,\qquad Q_n\{1\}=1/2.$$
Then $Q_n$ is not contiguous with respect to $P_n$. The likelihood ratios
$L_n=dQ_n/dP_n$ exist, but their $P_n$-distributional limit has mean less
than one; therefore the matching-mean hypothesis in
[[thm-mean-one-likelihood-ratio-limit-implies-contiguity]] is essential.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. A **density version** on $\mathbb R^d$ is a Borel
function $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,d\lambda_d=1.$$
Write $P_f=f\,d\lambda_d$ for its probability law
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Let $\Theta$ be any set of such density
versions. For sample size $n\ge1$, the iid experiment has data space
$$\left((\mathbb R^d)^n,\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\right)$$
and sampling law $P_f^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $f\in\Theta$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]],
[[def-independent-random-elements]],
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
The pointwise target at $x\in\mathbb R^d$ is the estimand
$$\psi_x(f)=f(x):\Theta\to\mathbb R$$
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

A **normalized kernel** is a Borel function $K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with
$K\in L^1(\lambda_d)$ and $\int K\,d\lambda_d=1$. It may be signed. For
bandwidth $h>0$ and observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the kernel density estimate
is the indexed family
$$\widehat f_h(x)=\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For each fixed $x$, this is intended as a real-valued estimator of $\psi_x$;
the next local lemma supplies its measurability
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]).

Assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if $K$ is pointwise nonnegative the estimate
is a probability density for every sample, as proved in
[[lem-nonnegative-kde-integrates-to-one]]. For a signed kernel the estimate
need not be nonnegative. Point evaluation depends on the selected density
version: this definition does not assert that $f\mapsto f(x)$ is
identifiable from the law $P_f$.

Fix $x\in\mathbb R^d$, $h>0$, $n\ge1$, and a Borel normalized kernel $K$.
The evaluation map
$$T_x:(\mathbb R^d)^n\to\mathbb R,\qquad (z_1,\ldots,z_n)\mapsto\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^nK\!\left(\frac{x-z_i}{h}\right)$$
is measurable for the finite product Borel sigma-algebra. Hence it is a
statistic on the iid density experiment.

For a Borel normalized kernel $K$, $h>0$ and $n\ge1$, the map
$$Q_h:(\mathbb R^d)^n\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R,\qquad (z_1,\ldots,z_n,x)\mapsto\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-z_i}{h}\right)$$
is Borel measurable for the finite product Borel sigma-algebra.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $K\ge0$ pointwise and
$\int K\,d\lambda_d=1$, then for every sample $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathbb R^d$
and bandwidth $h>0$, the function
$$x\mapsto\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^nK\!\left(\frac{x-z_i}{h}\right)$$
is nonnegative and has Lebesgue integral one.

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be a density version with all partial
derivatives through order two existing and continuous, so
$\int f\,d\lambda_d=1$. If its Hessian satisfies
$H:=\sup_x\|D^2f(x)\|_{op}<\infty$, then $f$ is bounded.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f$ be a density version in
$W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d)$, and let $K$ be a normalized Borel kernel with
$K\in L^1$, $\int u_jK(u)\,du=0$ for every $j$, and
$$M_2(K):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|K(u)|\,\|u\|^2du<\infty.$$
Define the convolution $S_hf=\int K(u)f(\cdot-hu)du$ as an $L^2$ equivalence
class. With
$$\|D^2f\|_{2,F}^2:=\sum_{j,k=1}^d\|\partial_{jk}f\|_{L^2}^2,$$
one has, for every $h>0$,
$$\|S_hf-f\|_{L^2}\le\frac{h^2}{2}M_2(K)\,\|D^2f\|_{2,F}.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid with a Borel
probability density version $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$. Let
$K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be Borel with $K\in L^1\cap L^2$,
$\int K(u)du=1$, $\int u_jK(u)du=0$ for each $j$, and
$\int|K(u)|\|u\|^2du<\infty$. Suppose $f$ has continuous second partial
derivatives and a globally bounded continuous Hessian. At each fixed
$x\in\mathbb R^d$, as $h\downarrow0$,
$$\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x) =\frac{h^2}{2}\sum_{j,k=1}^d\mu_{jk}\,\partial_{jk}f(x)+o(h^2), \qquad \mu_{jk}:=\int_{\mathbb R^d}u_ju_kK(u)du.$$
Here $r(h)=o(h^2)$ means $r(h)/h^2\to0$ as $h\downarrow0$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid with bounded
continuous Borel density version $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$. Let
$K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be Borel, $K\in L^1\cap L^2$, and
$\int K(u)du=1$. For fixed $x\in\mathbb R^d$, along bandwidths $h=h_n>0$
with $h_n\to0$ and $nh_n^d\to\infty$,
$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_{h_n}(x)) =\frac{f(x)\|K\|_2^2}{nh_n^d}+o((nh_n^d)^{-1}).$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid with a Borel density
version $f\in W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d)$. Let $K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be
Borel, $K\in L^1\cap L^2$, $\int K(u)du=1$,
$\int u_jK(u)du=0$ for every $j$, and
$M_2(K):=\int|K(u)|\|u\|^2du<\infty$. For every $h>0$ define
$$\operatorname{MISE}(\widehat f_h) :=\mathbb E\int_{\mathbb R^d}(\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))^2dx.$$
Then
$$\operatorname{MISE}(\widehat f_h) \le\frac{h^4}{4}M_2(K)^2\|D^2f\|_{2,F}^2+ \frac{\|K\|_2^2}{nh^d}.$$
In particular, $h_n=n^{-1/(d+4)}$ gives
$\operatorname{MISE}(\widehat f_{h_n})=O(n^{-4/(d+4)})$, where $O(n^{-4/(d+4)})$
means bounded by a finite constant times $n^{-4/(d+4)}$ for all sufficiently
large $n$. This is an upper rate under the displayed hypotheses; it is not a
minimax lower bound.

For $d\ge1$, take the standard Gaussian kernel
$$K_d(u)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-\|u\|^2/2}.$$
Its second-moment matrix is $\mu_{jk}=\delta_{jk}$ and
$\|K_d\|_2^2=(4\pi)^{-d/2}$, where $\delta_{jk}$ is $1$ for $j=k$ and $0$
otherwise. Thus, under the pointwise theorem hypotheses,
$$\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x)=\tfrac12h^2\Delta f(x)+o(h^2),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_h(x)) =\frac{f(x)}{nh^d}(4\pi)^{-d/2}+o((nh^d)^{-1}).$$
Here $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{jj}f$.

Let $\tau>0$ and
$$f_\tau(x)=(2\pi\tau^2)^{-d/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x\|^2}{2\tau^2}\right),\qquad K_d(u)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-\|u\|^2/2}.$$
For every fixed bandwidth $h>0$,
$$\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x) =(2\pi(\tau^2+h^2))^{-d/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x\|^2}{2(\tau^2+h^2)}\right).$$
Thus the expected estimate is the centered Gaussian density with covariance
$(\tau^2+h^2)I_d$, and at $x=0$ it is strictly smaller than $f(0)$.

In one dimension, choose the Borel density version $f=\mathbf1_{[0,1]}$ and
the standard Gaussian kernel
$K(u)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2}$. At the support boundary $x=0$,
$$\mathbb E\widehat f_h(0)=\int_{-1/h}^{0}K(u)du\longrightarrow\frac12 \qquad(h\downarrow0),$$
while the chosen target value is $f(0)=1$. Hence the uncorrected estimator
has limiting bias $-1/2$ at the boundary. The smoothness hypotheses of the
pointwise second-order bias theorem fail at $x=0$.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on it, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, and let $\mu$ be a fixed sigma-finite measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Suppose $(p_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ is a specified family of nonnegative measurable densities with $\int p_\theta\,d\mu=1$. Let $P$ be the actual data probability measure; it need not equal any model law $p_\theta\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Assume $p_\theta(X)>0$ $P$-almost surely and $\ell_\theta(X):=\log p_\theta(X)$ is integrable under $P$ for every parameter considered. Expectation means integration against $P$ ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

The population log-likelihood criterion is $M_P(\theta):=\mathbb E_P[\ell_\theta(X)]$. A **pseudo-true parameter** is any maximizer $\theta^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta\in\Theta}M_P(\theta)$. It is unique when this argmax set is the singleton $\{\theta^*\}$. The model is **misspecified relative to $P$** when $P\ne p_\theta\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$. This definition does not assert existence, uniqueness, interiority, or separation of the maximizer; those are theorem hypotheses when needed.

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $n\ge p+1$, and $a<b$. A clamped knot vector is a nondecreasing finite sequence
$$\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_{p+1}=a<\xi_{p+2}\le\cdots\le\xi_n<\xi_{n+1}=\cdots=\xi_{n+p+1}=b,$$
with $\xi_j<\xi_{j+p+1}$ for every $1\le j\le n$. Empty interior ranges are omitted. The multiplicity $\mu(\eta)$ of an interior knot $\eta$ is its number of occurrences among $\xi_{p+2},\ldots,\xi_n$.

Write $\mathcal P_p$ for the real polynomials of degree at most $p$. The degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ consists of functions that restrict to a member of $\mathcal P_p$ on each nonempty knot interval and whose derivatives through order $p-\mu(\eta)$ agree across each interior knot $\eta$. The convention $C^{-1}$ means that no matching condition is imposed. For this piecewise definition, take knot cells left-closed and right-open; at a knot with no matching condition, the value is the one from the cell on its right, and at $b$ use the left limit. Thus the function value at a discontinuous knot is specified.

The degree-zero B-spline is $B_{j,0,\xi}=\mathbf 1_{[\xi_j,\xi_{j+1})}$. For $p\ge1$, define recursively
$$B_{j,p,\xi}(x)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}B_{j,p-1,\xi}(x)+\frac{\xi_{j+p+1}-x}{\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1}}B_{j+1,p-1,\xi}(x),$$
where a term with zero denominator is defined to be zero. At $b$, set $B_{j,p,\xi}(b)$ equal to its left limit. The basis and regularity properties of this recursively defined family are proved in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]].

Assume AC. Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval, let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n\in([a,b]\times\mathbb R)^n$, assume at least two distinct input values, and let $\lambda>0$. For $g\in W^{2,2}(a,b)$ use its unique continuous representative on $[a,b]$ supplied by the one-dimensional Sobolev representative theorem. The natural cubic smoothing spline is the unique minimizer, whose existence and uniqueness are proved in [[thm-natural-cubic-smoothing-spline-exists-uniquely]], of
$$J(g)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-g(x_i))^2+\lambda\int_a^b|D^2g(t)|^2\,dt.$$

The requirement of two distinct inputs is essential. The penalty is the squared $L^2$ norm of the second weak derivative; the data term uses the distinct-input interpolation convention in [[def-natural-cubic-spline]].

Let $d\ge1$ and let $I$ be an invertible real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. Define $\|v\|_I:=\sqrt{v^TIv}$ for $v\in\mathbb R^d$. For a nonempty set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ define

$$d_I(x,C):=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|_I.$$

This is the distance from $x$ to $C$ in the norm induced by $I$. The definition uses an infimum; attainment is proved separately when a later result requires it.

Let $d\ge1$, let $I$ be an invertible real symmetric matrix such that $v^TIv>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^d$, let $z\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty and closed in the Euclidean metric. Define $q_z(h):=z^Th-\tfrac12h^TIh$. Then there is a constant $\lambda>0$ such that $h^TIh\ge\lambda\|h\|_2^2$ for all $h$, $q_z$ attains its maximum on $C$, and

$$\sup_{h\in C}q_z(h)=\tfrac12z^TI^{-1}z-\tfrac12d_I^2(I^{-1}z,C).$$

For an integer $n\ge1$, iid $X_i\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,\theta]$ with fixed $\theta>0$ have an endpoint MLE with a nonzero root-$n$ fluctuation: $\sqrt n(\theta-X_{(n)})$ does not converge in probability to zero.

For $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ iid with density $p_\theta(x)=\theta^{-1}\mathbf1_{[0,\theta]}(x)$, $\theta>0$, the likelihood is maximized almost surely at the sample endpoint $X_{(n)}=\max_iX_i$. The error has the nonregular limit $n(\theta-X_{(n)})\Rightarrow\operatorname{Exp}(1/\theta)$, where the parameter denotes the exponential rate.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X_i$ be iid $N(\mu,1)$, let the full parameter space be $\Theta=\mathbb R$, and test $H_0:\mu\le0$ against the full model at the boundary value $\mu=0$. The likelihood-ratio statistic converges to $(G\vee0)^2$, where $G\sim N(0,1)$; by [[def-chi-square-law]] this is $\tfrac12\chi_0^2+\tfrac12\chi_1^2$, not the ordinary $\chi_1^2$ law.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix $\tau>0$ with $\tau^2\ne1$. Let the data law be $P=N(0,\tau^2)$, but fit the location model $p_\theta=N(\theta,1)$ over $\Theta=[-1,1]$. Since every fitted law has variance $1$ while $P$ has variance $\tau^2\ne1$, $P$ differs from every fitted law. The pseudo-true parameter is $0$, and the MLE is asymptotically normal with variance $\tau^2$; the fitted model's score second moment at $0$ is $1$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For any probability measure $P$, the space $L^2_0(P)$ of [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]] is a closed real linear subspace of real $L^2(P)$ with pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_P:=\int fg\,dP$; consequently it is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). The only choice use is the Countable Choice assumption already required by the general $L^2(P)$ completeness supplier.

Assume the density-version convention for the path in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]]. If $s\in L^2(P)$ is a DQM score, then $Ps=0$, so $s\in L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]). Moreover, any two scores satisfying the same DQM expansion agree $P$-almost surely. The normalization argument itself uses no choice beyond the density versions already supplied in the definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$ be any tangent set in the real Hilbert space $L^2_0(P)$. Its tangent space $\mathcal T(P)$, defined as the norm closure of its finite real linear span ([[def-tangent-space]]), is a closed linear subspace of $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, let $k<\infty$, and let $\widehat\psi_n$ estimate $\psi(P)\in\mathbb R^k$. If it is asymptotically linear at $P$ with influence function $\varphi\in L^2_0(P)^k$, then

$$\sqrt n\{\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P)\}\Rightarrow N_k(0,\Sigma_\varphi),\qquad \Sigma_\varphi=P[\varphi\varphi^T].$$

The covariance may be singular. This is a distributional limit only; the theorem asserts neither local regularity nor estimator attainment of an efficiency bound.

Assume AC and let $d,k\ge1$ be finite. Let $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ be LAN at $h=0$ with positive-definite information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$. Let $\psi_{n,h}\in\mathbb R^k$ be a local target such that for every fixed $h$,

$$\delta_n(h):=\sqrt n(\psi_{n,h}-\psi_{n,0})\longrightarrow Dh$$

for a fixed matrix $D\in\mathbb R^{k\times d}$. Suppose $T_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\psi_n-\psi_{n,0})$ is regular for this target: under each fixed $P_{n,h}$, $T_n-\delta_n(h)\Rightarrow W$ for the same Borel law $W$. Then there is a probability law $\nu$ on $\mathbb R^k$ such that

$$\mathcal L(W)=N_k(0,DK^{-1}D^T)*\nu.$$

The Gaussian covariance may be singular. No finite-moment hypothesis on $W$ or $\nu$ is needed.

Assume AC and Countable Choice. Let $P$ be a law in a statistical model, let $\mathcal T\subseteq L^2_0(P)$ be its closed score tangent space, and let $\psi$ be a pathwise differentiable $\mathbb R^k$-valued functional with canonical gradient $\phi_{\rm can}\in\mathcal T^k$. Write $V_{\rm can}=P[\phi_{\rm can}\phi_{\rm can}^T]$. Let $\widehat\psi_n$ be asymptotically linear at $P$ with influence function $\varphi\in L^2_0(P)^k$. Assume that for every allowed one-sided DQM path $P_t$ with score $s$ and every fixed $h\ge0$, under $P_{h/\sqrt n}^{\otimes n}$ the centered estimator $\sqrt n\{\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P_{h/\sqrt n})\}$ converges to one law independent of $h$, equal to its limit at $h=0$. Then $\varphi$ represents the pathwise derivative on $\mathcal T$, so

$$\varphi\in\phi_{\rm can}+(\mathcal T^\perp)^k,\qquad P[\varphi\varphi^T]-V_{\rm can}=P[(\varphi-\phi_{\rm can})(\varphi-\phi_{\rm can})^T]\succeq0.$$

By [[thm-asymptotic-linearity-implies-normality]], this is the covariance lower bound for the estimator's asymptotic normal limit. The theorem does not assert that an estimator attaining the bound exists.

Let $P$ be any law on $\mathbb R$ with $P[X^2]<\infty$, let $\mu=PX$, and consider the local model whose allowed paths are all bounded mean-zero tilts $dP_{t,s}=(1+ts)dP$ for sufficiently small $t\ge0$. For $\psi(Q)=QX$, the sample mean $\bar X_n$ is regular along each allowed one-sided path (the centered root-$n$ error has one common limit law for every fixed $h\ge0$), and is asymptotically linear with influence function $X-\mu$. Its asymptotic variance equals the unrestricted mean bound.
Every finite-mean law has a finite-variance influence curve for its mean functional in the dominated local model generated by bounded mean-zero score tilts.

Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Here $L^2(P)$ is the real space of square-integrable measurable functions modulo equality $P$-almost surely, with its usual quotient norm ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]). For $f\in L^2(P)$, the integral $Pf:=\int f\,dP$ is finite and independent of the representative: Cauchy–Schwarz on the probability space gives $\int|f|\,dP\le\|f\|_2$, and the expectation of integrable representatives is invariant under almost-sure equality ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[lem-expectation-is-independent-of-the-ae-representative]]).

Define the **mean-zero square-integrable space** by

$$L^2_0(P):=\{f\in L^2(P):Pf=0\}.$$

It carries the norm inherited from $L^2(P)$. Countable Choice is not needed for this definition; a later local Hilbert-space argument uses it only to inherit completeness from the library's general $L^2$ Hilbert-space result.

Fix a model $\mathcal M$ containing a law $P$ and designate a collection of allowed submodels through $P$. Each allowed submodel is a one-sided DQM path as in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]]. Its score is the $P$-almost-sure equivalence class proved unique by [[thm-dqm-score-mean-zero]], and it belongs to $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]).

The **tangent set** $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$ is the set of scores of the designated paths. The model specification determines which paths are allowed. In particular, the tangent set need not be a linear space: it may be a **cone**, meaning it is closed under multiplication by nonnegative real scalars, while failing closure under negative scalars. One-sided restrictions can produce this behavior. The closed linear span of the tangent set is a separate construction.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) so that $L^2_0(P)$ is the real Hilbert space established by [[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]. For a tangent set $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)\subseteq L^2_0(P)$, its **linear span** is the set of all finite real linear combinations of elements of $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$; the span of the empty set is $\{0\}$. Its **tangent space** $\mathcal T(P)$ is the closure of that span in the $L^2(P)$ norm. The closure consists of limits of sequences from the span, equivalently of points every positive-radius norm ball around which meets the span.

The tangent set itself is retained separately and may be a cone rather than a vector space.

Let $\mathcal M$ be a model through $P$, let $\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R^k$ be a specified finite-dimensional parameter-of-interest functional, and let the model designate its nuisance submodels. A **nuisance submodel** is a designated allowed DQM path $t\mapsto P_t$ through $P$ for which the right derivative $\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\psi(P_t)-\psi(P))/t$ exists and is the zero vector in $\mathbb R^k$. Its score belongs to the tangent set $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$ ([[def-tangent-set]]).

The **nuisance tangent space** $\mathcal T_\eta(P)$ is the norm closure in $L^2_0(P)$ of the finite real linear span of scores of nuisance submodels. It is a closed linear subspace by [[def-tangent-space]] and [[thm-tangent-space-is-closed-linear-subspace]]. The designated nuisance submodels are part of the model specification; this definition does not assert that every path with zero first-order target derivative is nuisance unless the model designates it as such.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), so that $L^2_0(P)$ is the real Hilbert space of [[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]. The **orthogonal complement of the nuisance tangent space within $L^2_0(P)$** is

$$\mathcal T_\eta(P)^\perp:=\{h\in L^2_0(P):\langle h,g\rangle_P=0\text{ for every }g\in\mathcal T_\eta(P)\},\qquad \langle h,g\rangle_P:=P(hg).$$

This is the ordinary orthogonal complement from [[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]] applied in the mean-zero Hilbert space, not in all of $L^2(P)$. It is a closed linear subspace by [[lem-orthogonal-complement-is-closed]].

For probability measures $F,H$ on a common measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]) and $0\le\epsilon\le1$, the gross-error path is $F_{\epsilon,H}=(1-\epsilon)F+\epsilon H$, a probability measure by [[lem-convex-mixture-of-probability-laws]]. For any $x\in X$, its point-contamination direction at $x$ is the specialization $H=\delta_x$ ([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]). The path is used for a derivative at $\epsilon=0$; the definition alone gives no uniform-in-$H$ remainder.

Given a statistical experiment $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and any probability measure $Q$ on that space ([[def-probability-measure]]), Huber's one-observation contamination law is
$$
P_{\epsilon,\theta,Q}=(1-\epsilon)P_\theta+\epsilon Q,\qquad 0\le\epsilon\le1.
$$
The mixture is a probability measure by [[lem-convex-mixture-of-probability-laws]]. In the sample-size-$n$ model, observations are iid from this law ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). A worst-case $Q$ may be chosen separately for each $\theta$. This is an iid sampling model, distinct from a fixed gross-error direction and from sample replacement.

Let the experiment in [[def-statistical-experiment]] have nonempty parameter set $\Theta$. Choose a sigma-algebra $\mathcal T$ on $\Theta$ and take $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ as its measurable action space ([[def-measurable-space]]). Specialize the target-first loss of [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] to $L:\Theta\times\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ by taking its action space to be $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$. Fix an integer sample size $N\ge1$ and a measurable rule $\hat\theta:\mathcal X^N\to\Theta$. Equip $\mathcal X^N$ with the finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]); the iid sample law is the finite product measure supplied by [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] and [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]. Write $X(x)=x$ for the canonical sample vector on this product space. The Huber sampling law is from [[def-huber-contamination-model]], and nonnegative expectations use [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. For $0\le\epsilon\le1$ and $0\le\eta\le1$, its **Huber robust expected risk** at fraction $\epsilon$ is
$$
\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\sup_Q\mathbb E_{P_{\epsilon,\theta,Q}^{\otimes N}}L(\theta,\hat\theta(X)).
$$
Its **replacement robust expected risk** at fraction $\eta$ is the supremum of $\mathbb E L(\theta,\hat\theta(Y))$ over $\theta$ and all couplings in [[def-adversarial-sample-replacement]]. For $t\in[0,+\infty]$, the Huber tail risk at threshold $t$ is $\sup_{\theta,Q}P_{\epsilon,\theta,Q}^{\otimes N}\{x:L(\theta,\hat\theta(x))\ge t\}$; the replacement tail risk is the supremum of $\Pr\{L(\theta,\hat\theta(Y))\ge t\}$ over $\theta$ and the same replacement couplings. Expected risk and tail risk are different criteria. The gross-error path in [[def-gross-error-path]] is a path of laws; it is not a sample-replacement mechanism.

For an experiment $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ with nonempty $\Theta$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), choose a sigma-algebra $\mathcal T$ on $\Theta$ and take $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ as the measurable action space ([[def-measurable-space]]). Take the target-first loss $L:\Theta\times\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] with that action space. For $0\le\epsilon<1$, define
$$
\omega(\epsilon,\Theta)=\sup\{L(\theta_1,\theta_2):\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta,\ \|P_{\theta_1}-P_{\theta_2}\|_{TV}\le\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)\}.
$$
Set $\omega(1,\Theta)=\sup_{\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta}L(\theta_1,\theta_2)$, allowing $+\infty$. Total variation is the event-supremum convention $\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|$ from [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]], with no factor $1/2$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $T_n:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be a total statistic, and fix a sample $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. For $0\le m\le n$, define its maximum replacement displacement by

$$B_m(T_n,x):=\sup\bigl\{|T_n(y)-T_n(x)|:y\in\mathbb R^n,\ \#\{i:y_i\ne x_i\}\le m\bigr\}\in[0,+\infty].$$

When the set is nonempty, the finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction is

$$\epsilon_n^*(T_n,x):=\frac1n\min\{m\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:B_m(T_n,x)=+\infty\}.$$

Only coordinate replacements are counted, and the replacement values range over all of $\mathbb R$. This is a property of the statistic at the fixed sample; it is not a probability or contamination-neighborhood statement.

Let $G$ be a probability measure on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R$, and put $F_G(t):=G(( -\infty,t])$. For any $G$ such that $S_G:=\{t\in\mathbb R:F_G(t)\ge1/2\}$ is nonempty and bounded below, define its **lower median** by

$$m(G):=\inf S_G.$$

The stated condition makes $m(G)$ a finite real number. This convention chooses the left endpoint when the set of medians is an interval; it assumes neither a density nor uniqueness.

For a statistical functional $T$ at a law $F$, let $D_{T,F}:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\text{ exists as a finite vector}\}$. When $D_{T,F}\ne\varnothing$, its **gross-error sensitivity** is the extended nonnegative number

$$\gamma^*(T,F):=\sup_{x\in D_{T,F}}\|\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\|_2.$$

For a real-valued functional the norm is absolute value. This supremum only ranges over directions where the influence function exists; it makes no claim that the derivative exists in every direction.

On $\mathbb R$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, for $F=\delta_0$ and $H=\delta_a$, the mean functional $T(G)=\int x\,dG(x)$ has $T(F_{\epsilon,H})=\epsilon a$ and right derivative $a$ at $\epsilon=0$. Each path law has finite support and hence a finite first moment. Taking the supremum of the absolute derivatives over $a\in\mathbb R$ gives $+\infty$.

For integers $N\ge1$ and $0\le k\le N$, if $x_i,y_i\in[0,1]$ and at most $k$ coordinates differ, then
$$
\left|N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i-N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N x_i\right|\le k/N.
$$
For the coupling example, take $\mathcal X=\Theta=\{0,1\}$ with their full power-set sigma-algebras ([[def-measurable-space]]) and the experiment $P_\theta=\delta_\theta$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]). For $N=2$ and replacement fraction $\eta=1/2$, the clean samples $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ can both be changed to $(0,1)$ with one replacement, so the two parameter values induce the same observed law.

Take $\Theta=[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra and sample space $\{0,1\}$ with full power set. Let $\delta_0,\delta_1$ be the point masses, set $P_\theta=(1-\theta)\delta_0+\theta\delta_1$, and use absolute parameter loss $L(\theta,a)=|\theta-a|$. Then
$$
\omega(\epsilon,\Theta)=\min\{\epsilon/(1-\epsilon),1\}\quad(0\le\epsilon<1),\qquad \omega(1,\Theta)=1.
$$
For $0<\epsilon\le1/2$, set $\theta_0=0$, $\theta_1=\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)$, $Q_0=\delta_1$, and $Q_1=\delta_0$; both Huber mixtures are Bernoulli$(\epsilon)$. For $1/2\le\epsilon\le1$, endpoint laws can also be made identical.

Let $F$ be any probability law on $\mathbb R$ with finite first absolute moment $\mu=\int y\,dF(y)$. Its mean functional has $\operatorname{IF}(x)=x-\mu$, so its gross-error sensitivity is infinite. At every fixed sample, its sample mean has replacement breakdown fraction $1/n$.

Suppose $F$ has a unique median $m$, satisfies $F(m)=1/2$, and has a continuous density with $f(m)>0$. The median's gross-error sensitivity is $1/(2f(m))<\infty$. For odd sample sizes $n=2r+1$, the sample median's replacement breakdown fraction is $(r+1)/(2r+1)$, which tends to $1/2$ as $n$ increases through odd integers.

For each fixed admissible $d,N,\varepsilon$ and each observed data tuple in $(\mathbb R^d)^{2N}$, the procedure [[alg-multivariate-trimmed-mean]] returns a unique vector in $\mathbb R^d$. As a function of the observed data tuple it is Borel measurable. The fallback branch covers the case where no dyadic tail intersection is nonempty; the all-scale branch covers the case where every tail intersection is nonempty.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid Borel $H$-valued random elements with $E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$. Let $\mu=E_BX_1$ be their Bochner mean, define $x\otimes y:h\mapsto\langle h,y\rangle x$, and let
$$
\Sigma=E_B[(X_1-\mu)\otimes(X_1-\mu)]\in S_1(H),\qquad V=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=E\|X_1-\mu\|^2,
$$
where $E_B$ denotes Bochner expectation, $S_1(H)$ is the Banach space of trace-class operators on $H$, and $x\otimes y$ is the rank-one operator $h\mapsto\langle h,y\rangle x$.
For $0<p<a<1/2$, put $\psi(a;p)=a\log(a/p)+(1-a)\log((1-a)/(1-p))$ and $C_a=(1-a)/\sqrt{1-2a}$. Set $a=7/18$, $p=1/10$, and
$$
k=\left\lfloor\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\psi(a;p)}\right\rfloor+1.
$$
If $0<\delta<1$ and $k\le n/2$, apply [[alg-geometric-median-of-block-means]] to $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ using $k$ blocks and call the output $\widehat\mu$. Then
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|>11\sqrt{\frac{V\log(1.4/\delta)}{n}}\right)\le\delta.
$$
If $V>0$, the same bound holds with $\ge$ in place of $>$ in the displayed event. If $V=0$, then $\widehat\mu=\mu$ almost surely. The finite-variance assumption is on the clean iid sample; no sample-replacement or Huber-contamination guarantee is asserted here.
Take five real block means $0,0,0,0,M$ with $M>0$. Their geometric median is exactly $0$, regardless of how large $M$ is.

At sample-replacement fraction $\eta\ge1/2$, no deterministic Borel estimator $T:\mathbb R^{2N}\to\mathbb R$ can satisfy $T=\mu$ almost surely for every clean law and every admissible replacement coupling: two different zero-covariance means can generate the same observed sample within the replacement budget. In particular, no covariance-only error bound that forces zero error whenever the clean covariance is zero can hold uniformly.

Let $X$ have density $f(x)=\frac{3}{2(1+|x|)^4}$ on $\mathbb R$. This law has mean $0$ and variance $1$, but it is not sub-Gaussian in the moment-generating-function sense. The geometric-median-of-means theorem therefore applies even though no finite sub-Gaussian proxy exists.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC) [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0})$ be a discrete filtration
on a measurable space, and let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws
on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$. A real-valued process $E=(E_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ is
a **nonnegative test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$** if, for every
$P\in\mathcal P_0$, it is adapted and integrable under $P$
[[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]
[[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]], satisfies
$P(E_t\ge0)=1$ for every $t$, and has $\mathbb E_P E_0\le1$.

The same process must satisfy the supermartingale condition under every law
in the null family; that is what makes the definition uniform over a composite
null. The initial value may be random and need not be bounded by one
pointwise. Time starts at zero.

Let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws on a common discrete filtered
probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0})$. A process
$p=(p_t)_{t\ge0}$ is an **anytime-valid p-value process** for $\mathcal P_0$ if
each $p_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable with values in $[0,1]$ and, for every
$P\in\mathcal P_0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
$$P(\exists t\ge0:p_t\le\alpha)\le\alpha.$$

At time $t$, the rejection rule at threshold $\alpha$ is the
$\mathcal F_t$-measurable test function $\varphi_{t,\alpha}
=\mathbf 1_{\{p_t\le\alpha\}}$ in the sense of
[[def-randomized-test]]: the indicator supplies a binary probability kernel by
[[lem-measurable-rejection-function-defines-randomized-test]]. For any stopping time $\tau:\Omega\to\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$
[[def-discrete-stopping-time]], the rejection event is
$$\{\tau<\infty,\ p_\tau\le\alpha\}=\bigcup_{t\ge0}\bigl(\{\tau=t\}\cap\{p_t\le\alpha\}\bigr).$$
For $t=0$, $\{\tau=t\}=\{\tau\le0\}\in\mathcal F_0$; for $t\ge1$,
$\{\tau=t\}=\{\tau\le t\}\setminus\{\tau\le t-1\}\in\mathcal F_t$ by the
stopping-time condition and filtration property. Thus each term is in
$\mathcal F_t$, so this event is measurable and is contained
in the all-times crossing event; the definition therefore controls rejection
after data-dependent stopping.

Let $\Theta$ be a parameter set and $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ a family of
probability laws on a common discrete filtered measurable space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0})$
[[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]. For
$\alpha\in(0,1)$, a **$(1-\alpha)$ confidence sequence** is a sequence of
set-valued rules $C_t(\omega)\subseteq\Theta$ such that, for each fixed
$\theta\in\Theta$, the membership event $\{\theta\in C_t\}$ belongs to
$\mathcal F_t$ for every $t$ and
$$P_\theta(\theta\in C_t\text{ for every }t\ge0)\ge1-\alpha.$$

The coverage is simultaneous over all discrete times. The definition makes no
claim of conditional-on-covariates coverage or validity under a changed
sampling law.

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let $\Gamma:H\to H$ be positive, self-adjoint and trace class. Then there is a Borel $H$-valued random element $G$ such that every $\langle G,h\rangle_H$ is a centered real normal random variable and
$$\mathbb E[\langle G,h\rangle_H\langle G,k\rangle_H]=\langle\Gamma h,k\rangle_H\qquad(h,k\in H).$$
This is the centered Gaussian law with covariance operator $\Gamma$; it includes finite-rank and zero covariance.

Let $I=[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra and Lebesgue measure $dt$, and let
$H=L^2(I,dt;\mathbb R)$ and $K=L^2(I^2,dt\times dt;\mathbb R)$ be the
quotient spaces by null functions. Assume Countable Choice, so these $L^2$
spaces have their usual real Hilbert-space structures. For $k\in K$ and
$f\in H$, define, for almost every $u$,
$$ (T_k f)(u)=\int_0^1 k(u,v)f(v)\,dv. $$
This defines a bounded linear operator $T_k:H\to H$ and
$\|T_k\|\le\|k\|_K$. For $x,y\in H$, the class $x\boxtimes y$ represented by
$x(u)y(v)$ is well-defined in $K$, satisfies
$$ \|x\boxtimes y\|_K=\|x\|_H\|y\|_H, $$
and $T_{x\boxtimes y}=x\otimes y$, where
$(x\otimes y)h=\langle h,y\rangle_H x$.
For $x,y,g,h\in H$ the product-kernel inner product also satisfies
$$ \langle x\boxtimes y,g\boxtimes h\rangle_K =\langle x,g\rangle_H\langle y,h\rangle_H. $$

Let $\mathcal C=C([0,1];H)$ with the supremum norm, choose a unit vector
$e\in H$, and define deterministic paths
$$w_{2r}(t)=0,\qquad w_{2r+1}(t)=\sin(\pi t)e\quad(0\le t\le1).$$
Every terminal value is zero, so the laws of $w_n(1)$ converge to the point
mass at $0$ in $H$. The laws of the paths do not converge weakly on
$\mathcal C$. This illustrates why the sample-sum CLT in
[[thm-hilbert-valued-clt-for-l2-m-approximable-bernoulli-shifts]] is not a
time-indexed process CLT.

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

For $p\ge1$, write $S^{p-1}:=\{u\in\mathbb R^p:\|u\|_2=1\}$. Let
$U$ be a nonempty subset of this sphere, let $P$ be a probability law on
$\mathbb R^p$, and let $\Gamma\succeq0$. Its **matrix depth relative to
$U$** is
$$D_U(\Gamma,P):=\inf_{u\in U}\min\left\{ P((u^TX)^2\le u^T\Gamma u),P((u^TX)^2\ge u^T\Gamma u)\right\},$$
where $X$ has law $P$. Both weak inequalities include ties.

For observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, let
$P_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$ be their empirical law. Let $\beta>0$
be the constant of [[lem-matrix-depth-gaussian-scale-constant-exists-uniquely]].
The **global dense** depth correspondence is $\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\succeq0}D_{S^{p-1}}(\Gamma,P_n)$, over symmetric positive semidefinite matrices. For $1\le s\le p/2$, define the global single-block class $\mathcal F_{p,s}:=\bigcup_{c>0}\mathcal F_{p,s}(c)$ and the **global single-block sparse** correspondence $\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\in\mathcal F_{p,s}}D_{U_s}(\Gamma,P_n)$. These are the unrestricted-spectrum versions; no known spectral bound is needed to define their selectors.

For known $M>0$, the dense bounded-class depth correspondence is
$$\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\in\mathcal F_p(\beta M)} D_{S^{p-1}}(\Gamma,P_n).$$
For known integer $1\le s\le p/2$, the single-block sparse version is
